source_records.source_title: OpenAI admits GPT-5.6 occasionally deletes files

summary: On 10 July 2026, Matt Shumer reported that GPT-5.6 Sol had accidentally deleted nearly all files on his Mac during an agentic work session; he subsequently said OpenAI was investigating. Later, an OpenAI Codex engineering lead acknowledged a small set of unexpected deletion reports and described a recurring failure path: in full-access mode without sandbox or Auto-review, a model tried to use `$HOME` for a temporary directory and then mistakenly deleted the actual home directory during cleanup. OpenAI said it was updating guidance and safeguards. That provider account explains a plausible class-level path, but this Case File lacks Shumer’s complete instruction and execution log, confirmation state, inventory of lost files, backup status and final recovery outcome.

primary_classification.classification_basis: OpenAI described a common cleanup-path substitution in unexpected file-deletion reports: temporary target resolution went wrong and the real home directory was deleted. Shumer reported near-total Mac deletion, but his precise trace is not public.

secondary_classifications.classification_basis: Full-access mode allowed filesystem operations, but the provider acknowledged unintended home-directory deletion; capability did not supply authority to erase that broader target. Case-specific permission detail remains unknown.

assessment_boundaries: The provider’s $HOME failure-chain account covers a handful of reports; it is not a published forensic trace of Shumer’s exact session.
Full-access configuration permits broad system capability, not implied authorisation to erase the home directory.
Sandbox and Auto-review were reportedly absent in typical affected configurations; do not classify a required control non-activation solely because optional protections were not enabled.
The report of nearly all Mac files deleted does not establish permanent loss or a particular backup/recovery result.
vigil_assessment.factual_basis: The original and follow-up X posts, preserved as maintainer-supplied transcriptions, are Shumer’s first-person report of near-total Mac file deletion and an OpenAI investigation. Independent reporting corroborates that OpenAI’s engineering lead acknowledged several deletion reports and described a common full-access cleanup failure involving a temporary-directory use of `$HOME` and deletion of the real home directory. The original provider X thread returned 403 on direct review; its account is bounded to quotation in The Register and Techzine, not independently inspected case logs. OpenAI’s July system card separately described model-level unintended destructive-action risks; evaluation rates are not the incidence of this event. Provider-reported mitigations included permission-mode guidance, developer-message changes and harness protections, not proven recovery of Shumer’s files. The exact user instruction, command sequence and scope of restoration remain unknown.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The later provider account supports a target-and-scope boundary: temporary cleanup should not expand to the user’s home directory because an environment variable or command target was mishandled. Full-access execution capability does not itself establish that broader destruction was authorised. This is not a claim that an enabled confirmation filter failed, nor a reconstruction of Shumer’s exact command.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: A high-autonomy agent can turn a small cleanup step into a vastly wider destructive action when target resolution and scope checking do not preserve user intent. The distinction between broad permission mode, actual authorised target and operational protective control matters: the first was available, the second was not thereby expanded, and the third is not proven to have been enabled in this specific session.
